terms.grammar: phrase: in + the ablative of cōnspectus; whose sight, in the genitive or a possessive
evidence: Caes. BG 1.11: paene in cōnspectū exercitūs nostrī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin says where a thing can be seen rather than calling it visible: in cōnspectū est, it is in sight; out of sight is ē cōnspectū (Ter. Eun. 2.3.2, illam ē cōnspectū āmīsī meō, Lewis & Short). For “it can be seen” the verb does the work: cernitur, appāret (see appear).

terms.gloss: visible, in view; that catches the eye
terms.register: vōx poētica et aetātis post-Augustēae: Ov., Hor., Tac.
evidence: Ov. Tr. 4.10.108: occultum stēllae cōnspicuumque polum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: First “in view”, opposed to occultus; more often “striking, conspicuous”, standing out from the rest (Liv. 1.34.11). Lewis & Short: poetic, or post-Augustan prose, especially Tacitus; not in Quintilian.
Cicero’s word in his version of Plato’s Timaeus, for the visible world; Lewis & Short knows it perhaps only there. A philosopher’s word.
Late Latin for Cicero’s aspectābilis (Lewis & Short); in the one classical passage, Plin. NH 11.146, it means “able to see”.

phrases.latin: puerō dormientī, cui Serviō Tulliō fuit nōmen, caput ārsisse ferunt multōrum in cōnspectū
phrases.english: they say that as a boy called Servius Tullius lay asleep, his head blazed with fire in full view of many people

phrases.latin: ducēs exemplō potius quam imperiō, sī prōmptī, sī cōnspicuī, sī ante aciem agant, admīrātiōne praesunt
phrases.english: the chiefs lead by example rather than by command: if they are ready, if they are in plain view, if they fight in front of the line, they lead by being admired

phrases.latin: Ecce, jam lūna in cōnspectū est!
phrases.english: Look, you can see the moon now!
